history: The office cubicle was meant to set workers free. Robert Propst designed the Action Office for Herman Miller in the 1960s as a flexible, open workspace. Companies took the cheap part of the idea, the partitions, and packed people in. Propst spent his later years calling the result 'monolithic insanity'.

Capybaras, meanwhile, became famous for being unbothered. In 1982 a keeper at Izu Shaboten Zoo in Japan noticed them crowding into a puddle of warm water, and the zoo has given them a hot spring bath every winter since.

history: Around the year 890 a Norwegian chieftain named Ohthere visited King Alfred in England and described his home in the far north. Alfred's scribes wrote it down. Ohthere said he had sailed north partly for the walruses, 'because they have very fine ivory in their tusks', and he brought some as a gift.

The cod he would have fished are still caught off Lofoten every winter. Hung on wooden racks, the fish dries in the cold wind into stockfish, which keeps for years. It was one of the first things Norway ever exported.

history: Late in 1932 the Australian army sent soldiers with two Lewis machine guns into the wheat country of Western Australia to deal with some twenty thousand emus that were eating the crops. The same state was built on gold. Paddy Hannan's find near Kalgoorlie in 1893 started a rush, and in 1931 a seventeen-year-old named Jim Larcombe dug up the Golden Eagle, a nugget weighing more than 1,100 ounces, the largest ever found in Western Australia.

history: In the 1780s an Italian doctor, Luigi Galvani, found that a dead frog's leg kicked when he touched it with two different metals. He published in 1791 and called it 'animal electricity'. His nephew took the idea on tour, wiring up the bodies of executed criminals in front of paying crowds.

history: At the 1939 World's Fair in New York, Westinghouse showed off Elektro, a seven-foot aluminium man who could walk on command, speak about seven hundred recorded words, count on his fingers and smoke a cigarette. He later got a robot dog called Sparko.

The first robot with a real job was far less charming. Unimate, a one-armed machine, started work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961, lifting hot metal castings off a line so that people no longer had to.

history: Tutankhamun became pharaoh at about eight or nine and died at about eighteen or nineteen, around 1323 BC. He was a minor king, and that is why he is famous: his small tomb was overlooked by robbers, and Howard Carter found it nearly intact in 1922.

Among the thousands of objects inside was a dagger with an iron blade, made centuries before Egyptians could smelt iron. In 2016 tests confirmed that the metal came from a meteorite. The Egyptians had a phrase for the material: 'iron from the sky'.

history: The bald eagle has been on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. Benjamin Franklin was not a fan. In a letter to his daughter two years later he called it 'a bird of bad moral character' that steals fish from other birds, and said the turkey was 'a much more respectable bird'. He never proposed the turkey officially.

The longest inaugural address belongs to William Henry Harrison, who in 1841 spoke for nearly two hours in the cold, about 8,400 words. He died a month later, the shortest presidency in American history.

history: The phrase 'flying saucer' dates from June 1947, when a pilot named Kenneth Arnold reported nine shining objects near Mount Rainier and said they moved like a saucer skipped across water. Newspapers did the rest.

Two weeks later the army air base at Roswell, New Mexico, announced that it had recovered a 'flying disc' from a ranch, then said the next day that it was a weather balloon. In 1994 the Air Force gave a third answer: the wreckage came from Project Mogul, a secret programme of high-altitude balloons built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests.
